attributes: Per the tradition: a dybbuk is the soul of a dead person — characteristically one cut off with sins or obligations uncompleted — which, finding no rest, *clings* (the name is from the Hebrew for clinging) to a living body and possesses it, speaking through the host in the dead person's voice, confessing its story under rabbinic interrogation, and departing only through formal exorcism: the shofar, the ban, the commanded exit, classically through the host's little toe. S. Ansky's play *The Dybbuk* (written 1913-16), built from his ethnographic expeditions, gave the folklore its canonical literary form: the dead bridegroom Channon possessing his promised bride Leah on her wedding day, because the vow between the families was broken.

behavior_model: Triggers: a broken vow, an unconfessed sin, a death too sudden for its accounts -> the search for a host, characteristically someone bound to the dybbuk by the very obligation left unpaid. Needs: a body (its own is gone) and an ending — acknowledgment, restitution or judgment. Goals: the account closed. State changes: wandering -> clinging -> confessed -> departed: the exorcism liturgy is the state machine, and the tradition wrote it.
relationships: Defined by two relationships: the host (characteristically a bride, a relative, a vow-counterparty) and the exorcising rabbi — the tradition's dybbuk exists only between those two poles. attributes: Per the Qur'anic account: when God commands the angels to prostrate before the newly created Adam, Iblis refuses — 'I am better than he: Thou createdst me from fire, and him from clay' (sura 7:12; 38:76). The text specifies he 'was of the jinn' (18:50) though present in the angels' company — a distinction Muslim scholarship debates to this day. Cursed and reprieved at his own request until the Day of Judgment, he vows to waylay humanity 'from before them and from behind them', and the Qur'an is explicit about his limit: over God's sincere servants he has *no authority* (15:42) — his weapon is the whisper (waswas), suggestion only, and on the Last Day he will himself disown his followers: 'I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you answered me' (14:22).

personality.justification: The fire-born debater: he argues his case to God's face, negotiates his reprieve, and spends eternity making arguments at whisper-volume — inventive, proud, rhetorical, and bound by a limit he himself recites.

behavior_model: Triggers: a human moment of vanity, despair or heedlessness -> the whisper is placed. Needs: an answer — his system halts entirely at refusal; the tradition's believers are taught the counter-formula (seeking refuge) as a hard interrupt. Goals: the vindication of his founding argument, measured in answered whispers. State changes: honoured attendant -> refuser -> reprieved tempter -> self-disowning defendant at the Judgment: the Qur'an gives him the batch's most complete arc.
relationships: DISTINCT FROM SATAN, AS INSTRUCTED — with kinship bridged below: the Qur'an itself applies the title al-Shaytan to Iblis, so the traditions entangle the two even while the narratives (council prosecutor; fire-born refuser) are different stories from different corpora. In the Islamic lists he stands opposite the four great angels (Gabriel/Jibril chief among them) as the anti-figure of the system.
memory_model: Remembers: the clay and the fire — the original comparison is his permanent exhibit. Forgets: nothing on record. Misjudges: sincerity — his model assumes every refusal is a postponement; Qur'an 15:42 is the text's own statement of the variable he cannot price.
confidence_and_conflicts: The jinn/angel question is the record's honest centre: Qur'an 18:50 calls Iblis 'of the jinn', which classical and modern scholars reconcile with his presence among the angels in several ways (raised among them; 'jinn' as a class of angels in some readings; a jinni attendant) — no reconciliation is imposed here. The name's etymology (Greek *diabolos* via Syriac, or Arabic *balasa*, despair) is likewise disputed and flagged. Britannica 1911's Islam article and the Jewish Encyclopedia's comparative survey are this record's encyclopedia ground, both PD.
game_implementation: BrainKit: a persuasion-only architecture — an agent with zero direct-action verbs: he can only inject suggestions into other agents' deliberations (labelled, resistible, and logged), with a hard authority-cap against high-sincerity characters; the most mechanically honest tempter in the Atlas.
